On his twenty-fifth birthday Emmett Rusk sat across from Barrow with the ledgers spread between them like a map of a continent, and said that out of mines and rails and shipping lines and traction bonds he wanted only one thing: the Clarion, a dying city newspaper that lost money the way a torn sack loses grain. He moved into the building that week, installed Marsh to keep the books and Devlin to write whatever he pleased, and printed on the front page a signed statement of principles promising the people of the city the truth, tirelessly and without favor.

Within a year he had hired away every man on the rival paper's staff, from the editor to the copy boys, and celebrated with a brass band in the city room and a chorus line kicking among the desks. He went abroad to buy statuary and came back engaged to Adele, the governor's niece.

He had been a boy in a mining boarding house out west, and the winter a defaulted lodger's mine deed made the family rich, his mother sat at the kitchen table and signed him over to Barrow, who would raise him properly in the East. Out in the snow the boy heard the door and drove his sled into Barrow's stomach with all his small weight behind it, and was taken east anyway, past his father's silence and his mother's hand raised at the porch rail.

The marriage grew quiet in stages, all of them at breakfast: her questions, then his answers, then the shortening of both, then the morning she read a rival paper across from him and neither spoke at all. By then he had met Nora Kell on the street, a shopgirl who laughed at the mud on his coat, and had begun going up to her rooms in the evenings when the presses were rolling without him.

Mid-campaign for governor, the boss Halloran brought Adele up those same stairs and stood in Nora's parlor offering a bargain: withdraw, and the story stays out of print. Emmett refused, standing in a room with both women watching him, and lost the election in a landslide. Devlin asked to be transferred to another city. Adele took the divorce and the boy and the last of the family name.

He married Nora and decided she would be a singer, though she had no voice at all. She was humiliated at her debut, and Devlin, drunk in the office at four in the morning, began the savage review that Emmett took from the typewriter, finished in his own hand, printed, and then fired him for. Nora sang two more seasons, and then swallowed poison rather than sing a third, and he sat by the bed and told her, gently, that she need never sing again.

He shut her instead in the half-finished palace he called Silvermount, where she worked jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall too vast to heat. After a picnic on the beach among tents and hired musicians, after a quarrel that neither of them raised their voices in, she packed her trunks and drove away. He went into her bedroom and broke it apart, tore the hangings, swept the tables, and then stopped, holding a glass snow globe with a cottage inside it, and said, "Bluebell," and carried it out past the endless mirrors that showed him going and going and going.

He died alone in that house with the same word on his lips, and the globe rolled from his hand and broke on the floor. The newsreels recapped him: the mines, the paper, the two wives, the ruined campaign, the unfinished palace; they mentioned the last word and explained nothing.

They sent Nash to find out what Bluebell meant. A drunk Nora turned him out of a seaside nightclub before he had finished his first question. So he read Barrow's memoir, went back to Nora, and sat with Marsh in a boardroom and Devlin in a hospital ward and Colm the butler in the empty kitchens at Silvermount, and concluded at last that no single word ever explains a life. In the yard behind him workmen shoveled a child's sled into the furnace. The paint on it read Bluebell.

**Vehicles**

Rollo and Marcus drove the length of the city arguing about foreign drug laws, about what they call a quarter-pounder overseas, about how a country can be that civilized and still not know what to name a hamburger. Later that morning the same car held a boy named Del in the back seat, and Rollo turned to ask him a question with the gun still in his hand, and the gun went off, and Del had no head anymore, and the upholstery was a swamp. They drove it, dripping, to Warren's house in the suburbs, where a fixer in a tuxedo checked his watch, told them to strip, hosed them down in the driveway and dressed them in a T-shirt and shorts apiece, and they went to breakfast looking like tourists. Much later, a motorcycle idled at a curb with a girl on the back of it, and Denny took her out of the city with the sun coming up flat and yellow behind them.

**Hallways and Kitchens**

Outside a certain flat, waiting, the two of them argued about whether a man deserves to be thrown off a balcony for rubbing another man's wife's feet, and Rollo said a foot massage is nothing, and Marcus said nothing is nothing. Then they went in and Marcus quoted Ezekiel, slow, savoring it, about the tyranny of evil men, and they shot Tobin for skimming from Otis and took the briefcase off the counter. A fourth man came out of the bathroom firing a revolver and emptied it into the wall behind their heads, and Marcus stood in the plaster dust and said the word *miracle* and meant it. In another kitchen, weeks or days from that, Denny came back for the watch and found a submachine gun lying on the counter next to a jar of Pop-Tarts, and when the toilet flushed he lifted it, and Rollo came out zipping his fly and was dead before he understood the geometry of the room. Years before either kitchen, a hollow-eyed man home from a prison camp stood in a doorway and put a gold watch into a small boy's hand and explained where he had hidden it, and for how long, and why.

**Diners**

Two thieves at a formica table finished their coffee and decided, on impulse, between one sentence and the next, to rob the place; the girl stood on a booth screaming and the boy waved a pistol at the register. He came to Marcus's table last, and Marcus gave him his wallet and kept the briefcase, and talked to him the way you talk to a dog on a highway, and the couple walked out into the morning with a bag of strangers' money and their lives. At a different diner, one built to look like the past, waitresses dressed as dead film stars, Rollo took Nadia out for a five-dollar milkshake because Otis had told him to entertain her, and they took their shoes off and won the twist contest, and she held the trophy in the car like a baby.

**Otis's Bar**

They brought him the briefcase and he never opened it in front of them, because he was busy counting bills into the palm of an old boxer named Denny, explaining that Denny would go down in the fifth and stay down, that his boxing days were behind him either way. Denny took the money. Then Denny bet the money on himself, won the fight, hit his opponent so hard the man died on the canvas, and left the arena in a taxi with the driver asking him how it feels to kill a man.

**Rooms Where People Nearly Die**

Kip's living room: Rollo buying, cooking, floating, before his big night out. Kip's living room again, hours on: Nadia blue on the carpet, the black marker line drawn on her chest, the needle going in like a spear, her sitting up screaming. A motel room where Marielle, sorry, apologetic, admitted she had left the watch on the nightstand of his flat. And the basement under a pawnshop, where Denny and Otis, who had collided in the street and wrecked, hung bound in the dark; where Denny got loose, chose a sword off the wall upstairs, came back down while one of the captors was on top of Otis, and afterward Otis said they were square, provided Denny left town tonight and never came back.

The car took the corner on two wheels and Mr. Ash was still firing out the window, one hand on the wheel, the other punching holes in the morning. The robbery had lasted less than a minute. A guard had reached for something under a counter and after that there was nothing but glass and sirens, and now the street was behind them and the diamonds were in a bag on the floor and Danny Roarke, called Mr. Elm, was thinking that he had never once heard the signal he had been promised.

They dumped the car. Elm went over a fence and down an alley, and on Wharf Street he found a hatchback idling at a light with a man in it who looked like a schoolteacher. Elm dragged the door open and the man shot him in the stomach — a little silver thing from the glovebox, the last thing anybody expected — and Elm shot him twice and pulled his body onto the pavement and drove.

It was Ash who found him slumped over the wheel two blocks from the warehouse and carried him inside, and Elm screamed the whole way across the concrete. Ash sat down on the floor with him, put Elm's head in his lap, and pressed a folded jacket into the wound.

"You're not dying," Ash said. "Look at me. You're not going to die. I've seen men worse."

Weeks before, in a rented room above a laundrette, Pruitt had made him tell it forty times: the drug bust in the public toilet, the panic, the cistern, the dealer with the German shepherd. *Again. You're not reciting, you're remembering.* And when Danny finally told it to Bram and his son Cal and the flat-eyed man they called Mr. Ash, they laughed in the right places and Bram poured him a drink and said, welcome, son, and gave him a tree to be.

Mr. Birch came in shouting. He kicked a crate over and said the job had been a setup, that police don't sit in three cars on a Tuesday morning by accident, that there was an informer in the crew and he'd shoot him himself. Then he took the bag out through the side door and buried the stones somewhere in the weeds by the loading dock, because he trusted no one, and came back empty-handed.

Mr. Cedar arrived like a man returning from a picnic. He opened the boot of his car and lifted out a young patrolman, Doyle, bound and taped and blinking. Birch swore at him and left to find Bram. Cal went too.

The radio was on. Some sweet old song from before any of them were born. Cedar danced to it with a razor in his hand and cut off Doyle's ear and held it up conversationally, then poured petrol over the boy's chest and went looking for his lighter.

Elm shot him from the floor. Three rounds, and Cedar folded up and did not move again.

"Kid," Elm said, dragging air. "I'm a police officer. There are officers outside. They're waiting for Bram. Don't say a word."

There had been a breakfast, before, all of them squabbling over what that pop song was actually about — Ash insisting it was about the singer's brother, Cal insisting it was about nothing at all — and whether the waitress had earned the coins Ash left. And afterwards Bram handing out the names, and Birch complaining bitterly that Birch was a girl's tree, and Ren Vasco, who had walked out of prison that spring and come straight to them because they owed him nine silent years, laughing until he coughed.

Cal came back. He listened to Elm's account of Cedar. Then he walked over to Doyle, said, "Nothing personal," and shot him through the head.

Bram came in behind him, looked at the corpses, and pointed at Elm and said: there. There's your rat. That's the man.

Ash stood up and turned his gun on Bram, because he had carried Elm across that floor.

It took perhaps four seconds. Bram down, Cal down, Ash sitting against a pillar with his shirt going dark, and Elm breathing.

"Ash," Elm said. "I'm a cop. I'm sorry. I'm a cop."

The doors came off their hinges. Ash shot him, and then the light took Ash too.

Nina and Grady put the form letter on the table between them, the way you set down something that might go off. *Our records indicate that a patient has requested the removal of your presence.* Tobias read it twice, then drove to the clinic on Marsh Street and stood in Dr. Hallam's office with his coat still on, demanding the same thing, the whole thing, tonight if possible.

Two days before that he had gone into the bookshop for no reason and there she was, shelving art monographs, and she had looked up at him with a bright retail blankness. *Can I help you find something?* Behind her a young man with a technician's pallor was laughing at whatever she'd said before Tobias came in. She called him Peck. She touched Peck's sleeve. Tobias stood in poetry for eleven minutes and then walked out into the sleet.

They gave him a cardboard box and told him to fill it. Everything connected to her: the mixtape, the toothbrush, the postcard from the drive-in, the noodle-house chopsticks she'd stolen, a mitten, a photograph of her laughing on ice. The clinic needed the objects to map where in his skull she lived. That night two technicians let themselves into his flat, Dell with the headset and Peck with the machine, and while Tobias went under Peck quietly slid the mitten and the photograph into his own jacket pocket, because he had somewhere to be with them later.

The last thing before the bookshop was the car. She came home at two in the morning smelling like a wet distillery and told him the dent had already been there. He said nothing, which was his whole vocabulary by then, and she screamed that his silence was the cruelest room she had ever lived in, and then she took her bag off the hook and went out and did not come back.

Inside his own head he could walk. The technicians were pulling threads and he followed them, watching the recent months go dark: the dent, the silence, the slammed door, all of it thinning like breath on glass and gone. He was almost grateful. Meanwhile in the flat Dell was passing a joint to Rosa the receptionist, both of them sprawled on Tobias's bed with the map beeping unattended, his memories rearranging themselves like furniture in an earthquake.

Before the car there had been a year of low weather. Bottles behind the radiator. *You don't want me, you want to be needed by me.* Every kindness itemized and returned with interest. They had gotten very good at it, the way people get good at a language they hate.

Hallam came at three in the morning to re-map, furious, tie askew. Rosa kissed him in the hallway and he let her, and then his wife came in behind him and said, with terrible gentleness, that Rosa had had her own six months with him removed last spring and signed the consent herself. Down in the flat, deeper in, Tobias had reached the good ones — the frozen river, the noodle house steam, the drive-in — and he was doing something the machine had no protocol for: he was dragging her into rooms she'd never entered, hiding her in his childhood, under a desk at work, anywhere the beam wasn't looking.

Before all of that: a beach party at the end of the rail line, a girl who said *let's break into that house*, and the two of them in an empty shore house with sand on the floorboards, falling in love over two years without noticing they'd started. And at the end of the erasure that was the only room left standing, the same bare house, the same sand, and she said, *I know, I know, I'm being erased, meet me in Montauk,* meaning the beach, meaning the cold sand, and he said okay.

He woke with nothing missing that he could name. He went to the station instead of work, took the train to the coast, and there was a woman on the frozen sand, and he said something stupid, and she laughed. They drove back to the city and she asked him up.

Then Rosa quit and mailed every file, every tape, to every patient on the books. They sat on her floor and listened to their own voices flaying each other. She ran out. She came back. She said, *So what?*

The motel room had a number on the key and nothing else Martin recognized. He sat on the bed with the phone against his ear and told the anonymous caller about Elias Prine, the way he always told it: the claimant who forgot, the wife with the insulin, the tests she set him. He was still talking when the voice on the line gave him a name. Gil Marsh. And an address, a dead building on the edge of the industrial road. Martin wrote it on his palm.

Before that, in a field at dusk, he burned her hairbrush and her paperbacks in an oil drum and waited to feel it leave him. Grief needs a yesterday to stand on. He watched the pages curl and by the time the ash cooled he was reading the note in his own hand that told him what he had just done.

In the derelict basement he beat Gil Marsh until the man stopped covering his face, then knelt on his chest and took his throat in both hands. He photographed the body twice, so there would be no argument. As Gil died he whispered a word: *Elias*. Martin had no place to put it. He changed into the dead man's suit because his own shirt was ruined, and took the keys to the sports car parked outside.

Before that, a year earlier, a plainclothes cop named Roy had driven him to a rented room and stood in the doorway while Martin did what he had spent months preparing to do. The real man, the second man, the one from the bathroom. Roy said, *You did it. It's over.* Martin believed him for eleven minutes. Then he asked Roy where they were going.

Roy came for him in the parking lot and said Gil Marsh had sold pills to teenagers and nothing more. Said Martin had already avenged his wife, a year ago, with Roy's own hands helping. Said the Prine story wasn't a case file, it was a mirror; that Martin was Elias, that Martin's wife had tested him with injection after injection until she stopped waking up. Martin listened. Then he burned the photographs of Gil in the ashtray, wrote *he is lying to you* across the Polaroid of Roy's face, and copied the licence plate off Roy's car onto the back of his hand.

A room with a fluorescent hum. A doctor's mouth says *weeks*, and Aaron Vale, who has spent his life proving things, cannot prove otherwise. His heart is a bad theorem.

Water. Chlorine, the blue rock of it, a woman doing an inelegant sidestroke in the slow lane. He drops into the water beside her as if by accident, though nothing about it is accident: there is a folder in his car with her address, her maiden name, the make of the car she no longer owns. Lena. She laughs at something he says about the lane markers. He has rehearsed the joke.

Wes Tarrow stands at the desk of a police station with his hat in his hands and says the words, and they take him, and the door of the cell is a sound he already knows.

Della's hand on the small of Aaron's back, insistent, warm. *There's still the sperm we froze. Sign, and I'll do the rest, you won't have to be here for it.* Estranged is a legal word; it does not cover a wife who wants your child while you are dying.

The motel sign reads VACAN, the last letter dark. Aaron parks and holds the gun in his lap for eleven minutes and then walks across the gravel, and when the door opens on a man in an undershirt, Aaron shoots him in the shoulder and hears his own voice, thin, absurd: *Run. Go on. Run.*

Nita listens to Wes pray at the kitchen table and it is not the praying that frightens her, it is the way the vein moves in his temple while he does it. He has a job. He coaches ten-year-olds on a dirt diamond and calls them *son* and does not drink. She dreads him the way you dread weather.

Cocaine again, after all those years, and the beautiful arithmetic of it: how much, how fast, how soon. Lena does it methodically, like a woman clearing out a house.

Sunlight on a hospital ceiling, and Aaron wakes and understands, before any word is spoken, that he is alive. Something in his chest is working. It is working better than his ever did. He weeps and the nurse says everyone does.

The crossing, the low sun, the pickup. A man and two small girls. The truck slows and turns back and idles a moment in the road, and then it goes.

*It's his heart,* Aaron says. *Doug's.* Lena's face empties. She puts him out onto the porch with his shoes in his hand and he sleeps in the car, and at four in the morning she opens the door and stands there and doesn't say anything and he comes in.

A corridor, plastic chairs. Someone tells Lena all three. She asks them to say it again, because surely they mean one, surely they have miscounted.

Della's kitchen. *I don't want it,* Aaron says. *Not the child, not any of it. I'm sorry.* He takes two suitcases. She does not scream, which is worse.

Wes walks out of the prison early and out of Nita's life and out of the faith that held him like a fist, and takes a job stripping beds at a motel four hundred miles from anyone who knows his name.

Doug's heart, in a box of ice, in a car with its lights going.

*I want him dead,* Lena says. She says it in a diner, over eggs. She says it the way she might ask for the check. Aaron buys a gun from a man in a parking lot and learns to load it from a video.

A suburban Sunday: Lena, clean six years, watching Doug chase the girls across the lawn with the hose, thinking that this is what it was all for, this ordinary green afternoon.

The other motel, later. Wes has followed them; he stands bleeding in the doorway and says, *Do it right this time.* And Aaron looks at the two of them, and turns the barrel around, and does the only honest thing he can think of.

The heart fails on the table. It was never his.

Wes drives home to his wife.

Lena drives home pregnant, and alone.

Snow came early that year, and in the first white of it two cars kissed bumpers on Alvarado and two drivers stood shouting in the falling quiet, and everything that follows had already happened by then.

But start with the gun. Nadir counted bills onto the glass case while the dealer drawled *yalla yalla* at him and laughed, and Sahar, seventeen, watched her father's ears go red and said nothing until they were in the car. Start with the same week Trey and Kwame stepped out of a doorway in front of the prosecutor Halstead, took his keys, took his car, and drove it laughing through three red lights.

Later — months later, on a shoulder of frontage road with the sun coming up — Detective Isaiah Reece would lift a tarp off a body and see his brother's face, and there would be a sound out of him that the uniforms pretended not to hear.

Officer Boyle pulled over the Hobarts that night because the wife was white and the husband was not, and he put his hands on Renee where Clay could watch, and then he let them go with a warning about their taillight. In the morning his partner Voss stood in front of their commander asking for a car of his own, any car, because he could not sit another shift beside a racist. The commander said the paperwork would embarrass him. Voss took the paperwork.

Halstead's wife Paula stood over the locksmith Mateo while he changed her locks and said loudly, to no one, that he'd be selling her keys to his gang by nightfall. Mateo finished the job and drove to Nadir's shop and put a new lock on that door too, and told Nadir the door itself was broken, the frame was rotten, it needed replacing, and Nadir said this was the con, this was always the con, and threw him out into the street.

At his mother's kitchen table Reece would sit with his hands open and hear her say: not once. Not one time did you go and look for him. You have a badge and you never once went to look.

Boyle spent his day off on hold, then in a chair across from a clerk named Delia Frank, explaining his father's lungs, and she said the procedure was experimental and the answer was no, and he leaned across her desk and said please, and she said the answer was no.

That night Nadir's shop was emptied and smashed, every shelf, and the insurer read the locksmith's note about the door and paid nothing.

Renee Hobart hung upside down in a car folded around a pole with gasoline running toward the flame, and a cop crawled in through the broken glass and cut her free and dragged her out with her hair in his fists, and when she got her eyes open she saw whose hands they were, and he saw her see.

Trey and Kwame ran down a shopkeeper named Pham and put him in the back and left him breathing at the hospital doors. Clay Hobart, taking back his own stolen car, was surrounded by drawn pistols, and it was Voss who stepped into the muzzle-line saying the man lives here, look at his face, he lives here. Then Clay drove Trey away at ninety miles an hour and threw him out of the moving car into a hedge.

Nadir waited outside Mateo's house until dark with the gun in his coat, and when Mateo came out he raised it, and a small girl in a pink coat ran across the lawn into her father's arms, and Nadir fired. Rosie was untouched. Sahar had bought blanks. Nadir sat down on the curb and wept and decided his daughter was an angel.

Voss picked up a kid hitchhiking in the cold, liked him, laughed with him, and then the kid reached into his pocket and Voss shot him in the chest and drove into the hills and burned the car with him in it and walked home.

Paula fell down her own stairs with nobody in the house and lay there until Alba came, and told her housekeeper she was the only friend she had.

Trey opened Pham's van and found twelve people packed inside, and drove them to the docks, and cut the zip ties, and let them run.

Then the snow, and the shouting, and the shouting.

The dogs first, because the dogs are the hinge of it.

Ruben found out about Tigre by accident: his brother Nestor's rottweiler went for a neighbour's mongrel and did not stop, and Ruben stood in the alley with his mouth open and understood that he was looking at money. He began entering the dog in the fights behind the sawmill and Tigre won and won. In the last of them the promoter Chaco, sick of paying, drew a pistol and shot the dog in the ring; Ruben put a knife into Chaco's side and ran out into the street with Pipo pulling him by the sleeve. Later, at a junction, a vagrant named Cardo reached into a wrecked car and dragged the bleeding animal out by the collar, and carried it home to his yard, and nursed it for weeks on rice and horsemeat until it stood again among his own loose pack of strays. He came back one evening to find every one of those strays dead in the dirt and Tigre sitting quietly in the middle of them. He pressed his gun to the dog's skull and held it there a long time and could not fire. In another part of the city Celine Vaz's lapdog Chispa fell through a gap in the floorboards of a flat so new the paint still stank, and Hector tore up the whole floor plank by plank looking for it, and did not find it.

Now the rooms, because everyone in this story is trying to leave one.

Ruben's mother's house held five of them and a baby: Nestor, Alma, the child, the old woman, himself, all breathing the same warm sour air. Nestor came in from robbing a pharmacy at three in the morning and hit Alma for the noise the baby made, and Ruben lay in the next room whispering to her through the wall that they should go, tonight, anywhere. Hector left a wife and two daughters in one apartment and installed Celine in another, with a window that looked directly at her own face on a billboard across the avenue. Celine woke instead in a hospital room with her leg pinned together like a broken chair, asking about the dog. The leg went bad; they took it off above the knee; the billboard came down within the month and the wall behind it was grey and streaked. Cardo's room was a shed at the edge of the wasteland with newspaper on the windows, and it was there he chained Sergio to a pipe rather than shoot him, and there he brought Elian, the half-brother who had paid for the killing, and stood the two of them face to face and laid a loaded pistol on the floor between them and walked out. He had taken money from both. Later he broke a window in a clean small flat that was not his, spoke twenty minutes into his daughter Perla's answering machine, and left with her photograph in his coat.

And last the money, since that is what all of it was for.

Ruben hid his winnings in a coffee tin under a loose brick and paid two men to break Nestor's ribs, and Nestor answered by taking Alma, the baby and the coffee tin and vanishing before dawn. Nestor was shot dead some months after that, coming out of a bank with a bag in his hand, and at the graveside Ruben asked Alma one final time to come away with him, and she looked at the hole and said no. Elian's envelope was thick and smelled of cologne; Sergio's, offered later from a chained man's pocket, was thicker. Cardo, who had once carried a rifle in the mountains for no wages at all, counted neither. He watched his wife lowered into the ground from behind a row of parked cars, followed his grown daughter home at a distance of forty metres, and afterwards shaved his beard, put on clean clothes, stacked every note he owned on Perla's kitchen table, and went out into the wasteland with the dog walking loose at his side.

There is a moment — hold it, because I will come back to it — when a gun is in my mouth and the barrel tastes like everyone's fingers, and a man I have loved and invented is kneeling over me on a landing, telling me this is the greatest moment of my life, and I am about to disagree with him by pulling the trigger and blowing a hole through my own cheek.

Before that, though, there was insomnia. Three years of it. My job was to fly out to wrecks and price the recall, multiply the units by the probable settlement, and report that it was cheaper to let people burn. I could not sleep. Then in a church basement I sat in a circle of men dying of things I did not have, and a man named Bob held my head against his chest, and I wept, and that night I slept like a stone in a river.

Ada Vey ruined it. She turned up at blood parasites and then at brain disease, tourist-eyed, smoking outside afterwards, faking every tear, and because she was lying I could not lie, and the sleep went out of me again.

On a flight I met Rex Marrow, soap salesman, and pocketed his card without knowing why. Two weeks later my flat detonated — every catalogue lamp, every unit of shelving, blown out over the parking lot — and I stood in a phone booth and called him. He took me to a house at the edge of the industrial district with no proper windows and rain coming through three floors.

Outside the bar he said: I want you to hit me as hard as you can. So I did, and he opened my lip, and we knelt in the gravel laughing with blood in our teeth.

Here is the other thing I promised. The recruits bring Ada up the stairs of the tower with their hands on her arms and their shaven heads gleaming, and they set her down in front of me and ask if there is anything else, sir, and I tell them to go. Her mascara has run. My cheek is packed with gauze and I speak like a man with a mouthful of gravel. We stand at the window and take each other's hands and the debt-record towers go down one after another like men kneeling.

But first the club. What began as two men in a car park hardened into Wednesday nights in a basement with rules — two men to a fight, no shirts, no shoes, the fight is over when one man goes limp. More came each week than the week before. Ada overdosed on pills and Rex carried her into the derelict house and after that they went at each other every night, loudly, through the wall, and I lay in the dark hating them both.

He was rendering fat stolen from a liposuction clinic's dumpster into soap and selling it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He held my hand down and poured lye on it and would not let me go into my cave, my ice cave, my power animal — stay with the pain, he said, this is the only real thing.

I walked into my director's office with my own face already ruined and blackmailed him into paying my salary to stay home.

Then Rex renamed it Havoc, filled the house with shaven men who spoke only when asked, and sent them out to burn corporate art and shear the heads off statues. He took the wheel on a wet road and steered us into oncoming traffic and let the car roll down the embankment, and afterwards he was simply gone.

A man called Ogden was shot dead on an errand and I began trying to end it. City to city, and in every city the same basement, and in every basement men who called me Rex Marrow, sir.

That is how I learned what I was. That he moved while I slept. That Ada had never been with anyone but me — she confirmed it in a diner, exhausted, saying your name is Rex, you told me yourself.

The charges were already in the parking structures when I found them. I could not defuse them. He came down the stairwell for me, and the gun went in my mouth, and now you know exactly where we are standing, and whose hand she is holding.

Then in a church basement I sat in a circle of men dying of things I did not have, and a man named Bob held my head against his chest, and I wept, and that night I slept like a stone in a river.

Ada Vey ruined it. She turned up at blood parasites and then at brain disease, tourist-eyed, smoking outside afterwards, faking every tear, and because she was lying I could not lie, and the sleep went out of me again.

On a flight I met Rex Marrow, soap salesman, and pocketed his card without knowing why. Two weeks later my flat detonated — every catalogue lamp, every unit of shelving, blown out over the parking lot — and I stood in a phone booth and called him. He took me to a house at the edge of the industrial district with no proper windows and rain coming through three floors.

Outside the bar he said: I want you to hit me as hard as you can. So I did, and he opened my lip, and we knelt in the gravel laughing with blood in our teeth.

Here is the other thing I promised. The recruits bring Ada up the stairs of the tower with their hands on her arms and their shaven heads gleaming, and they set her down in front of me and ask if there is anything else, sir, and I tell them to go. Her mascara has run. My cheek is packed with gauze and I speak like a man with a mouthful of gravel. We stand at the window and take each other's hands and the debt-record towers go down one after another like men kneeling.

But first the club. What began as two men in a car park hardened into Wednesday nights in a basement with rules — two men to a fight, no shirts, no shoes, the fight is over when one man goes limp. More came each week than the week before. Ada overdosed on pills and Rex carried her into the derelict house and after that they went at each other every night, loudly, through the wall, and I lay in the dark hating them both.

He was rendering fat stolen from a liposuction clinic's dumpster into soap and selling it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. He held my hand down and poured lye on it and would not let me go into my cave, my ice cave, my power animal — stay with the pain, he said, this is the only real thing.

I walked into my director's office with my own face already ruined and blackmailed him into paying my salary to stay home.

Then Rex renamed it Havoc, filled the house with shaven men who spoke only when asked, and sent them out to burn corporate art and shear the heads off statues. He took the wheel on a wet road and steered us into oncoming traffic and let the car roll down the embankment, and afterwards he was simply gone.

A man called Ogden was shot dead on an errand and I began trying to end it. City to city, and in every city the same basement, and in every basement men who called me Rex Marrow, sir.

That is how I learned what I was. That he moved while I slept. That Ada had never been with anyone but me — she confirmed it in a diner, exhausted, saying your name is Rex, you told me yourself.

The charges were already in the parking structures when I found them. I could not defuse them. He came down the stairwell for me, and the gun went in my mouth, and now you know exactly where we are standing, and whose hand she is holding.

The old man's window was open two inches, enough for the sirens. He didn't look down. "Nothing keeps," he said to the young man on his sofa, who had come about a lease and stayed for tea. "Not stone, not grudges, not you. Time eats it all and doesn't chew. People think they're building something. They're only holding a shape for a while."

Below, the police brought the two of them out of the club's side door, one on each arm apiece, the way you carry furniture. Cort's arm hung wrong and he was screaming about it, or about something. Jonah went quietly, red to the wrists, his shirt stuck to him. A woman filming from the kerb caught the exact second the door swung shut behind them.

Inside, four minutes earlier, Jonah had picked up the fire extinguisher because it was there, because his friend was on the floor making a sound Jonah had never heard a man make, because the man standing over Cort had said *say that again*. He brought it down and down. A thin man in a good coat watched from six feet away with his hands in his pockets, mildly, the way you watch weather. Nobody pointed at him. Nobody knew to.

Before that, Cort had gone through the Pit room by room with Lise's name in his mouth like a stone. Bad light, bass in the ribs. He found a shaved head that matched what he'd been told and got two hands into the collar, and the man turned and took Cort's arm and folded it against the joint until it went, and the noise of the club swallowed the crack whole.

Outside, on the pavement by the tape and the ambulance, two men had appeared at Cort's shoulder while he was still shaking. They knew things. Everyone in that postcode knew things. They wanted forty and they took twenty and they said: they call him the Adder, he drinks at the Pit, go now before he doesn't. Jonah said it was rubbish. Cort was already walking.

They had come out of the party together, Cort still glassy, Jonah pulling him by the sleeve because Lise wasn't answering, and found the street full of light. The stretcher going up into the van. The blanket. One shoe on the trolley beside her and the other, Jonah realised later, never found at all.

Nobody saw it except a man who came into the underpass, saw, and reversed out again like film run backwards. By then she was against the concrete and the Adder had a fist in her hair and was using the wall the way you'd use a tool, unhurried, and the tiles were shining under the strip light.

She hadn't wanted to cross four lanes at that hour so she took the steps down. She was three metres in when she saw the tall woman on her knees, the mascara, the man's belt already off, and the man turning his head towards Lise with a kind of pleasure at the arithmetic of it.

She had left the party alone. She'd watched Cort do the rounds of the kitchen — cans, then pills, then a girl in a green dress whose waist he held like a banister — and she had stood there with a warm drink and a thing she hadn't told him yet and thought: no. She got her coat. She didn't say goodnight.

On the way there the three of them had swayed together in the last carriage, Jonah insisting nobody has good sex sober, Lise saying that explained a great deal about Jonah, Cort laughing and drinking and Lise taking the can off him twice and both times letting him have it back.

That afternoon she had sat in the park with a paperback she wasn't reading, sprinklers ticking over the grass, children screaming happily in the wet, one hand flat and quiet on her stomach.

That morning, alone in the flat, she had waited the three minutes on the edge of the bath and then looked, and looked again.

The night before, in bed, she'd told Cort about the dream she kept having, the long red tunnel with no end to it, and Cort had said maybe it's Jonah's flat, and she'd hit him with a pillow, and they had both laughed until they couldn't breathe.

All night the helicopters came low over the valley, dusting the city for medfly, their rotors combing the rooftops of every street where any of this happened. People shut their windows and slept badly.

In the hills, Dr. Neil Hartigan buttoned a clean shirt while his wife Bess, still smelling of turpentine, chose earrings for the dinner party they were giving that evening.

Downtown, before the ovens cooled, the baker Otto Kemp wrote an order on a card in his flat block letters: chocolate, one boy, name of Charlie Rill, eight years old, pickup Saturday.

Charlie never made Saturday. Walking to school he stepped off the curb and a waitress named Rhona, late for her shift, knocked him flat. He sat up, said he was fine, refused her offer of a ride, and walked home carrying his lunch bag.

By afternoon he was asleep in a way that would not end. Grant and Elaine Rill sat in the hospital corridor while doctors said the word *coma* as if it were a temporary weather condition.

On the second day Grant's father Duff appeared with a cigarette he wasn't allowed to smoke and told his son, in a room full of vending machines, about a woman in 1957 and the years of silence that followed.

The cake sat in the case, uncollected, unpaid. Otto Kemp dialed the Rill number at eleven at night and said, *You forgot Charlie,* and hung up, and did it again the next night, and the next.

Across town Cheryl sat cross-legged on her living room floor with the phone at her jaw, telling a stranger what she was wearing, while her husband Stu watched the television with the sound off and his jaw working.

That Friday Stu and three friends drove out with rods and beer to the Naches, and in the shallows below the rocks they found a girl face down, naked, her hair moving with the current.

They talked it over. They tied her ankle to a root so she wouldn't drift, and they fished two more days, cooked trout on the bank, drove home Sunday night, and only then did somebody call the sheriff.

Vern told his wife Iris, who painted her clown face in a mirror before children's parties, and Iris stopped with the greasepaint half on and said she did not know him, that none of them were men.

In the club on Fourth, Vida sang until one in the morning under a pink spot, and out in the hills her daughter Bee played cello alone in an empty house, the same eight bars over and over.

Officer Rowe, who was seeing a woman named Nan on his days off, needed an alibi for his wife Peg, so he drove the family dog to a suburb miles away and let it out and told the children it had run off.

Nan's ex-husband Cass flew a spray helicopter and had heard she had someone new. He let himself into her house with his old key and took a saw to her bed, her table, her chairs, sawing until nothing would stand.

Ike and Dot house-sat the Hartigan place, and while the owners were out Dot lay on the tile in the guest bath with bruises drawn in eyeshadow and lipstick, and Ike stood over her with the camera and told her to hold still, to look dead.

At the dinner party Bess drank too much wine and told everyone about the art class she'd modelled for, nude, at twenty-two, and then about the man she'd slept with after, and Neil stood up so fast his chair fell and shouted at the guests until they left.

Charlie died at 4:20 in the morning. That afternoon Grant and Elaine drove to the bakery and pounded on the glass, and Otto Kemp unlocked the door, sat them down, tore open warm rolls, poured coffee, said *eat something,* and wept with them until the streetlights came on.

Vida came home at two and fell asleep in her clothes, and Bee looked at her, went out to the garage, pulled the door down, started the car, and sat in the driver's seat with her hands in her lap.

At a picnic in the dry hills, Stu followed a girl away from the blankets, and when she turned, he brought a rock down on her head, once, and then again.

Then the ground moved. The whole city shuddered for eleven seconds, and by evening every death, every wreck, every siren from that day was folded into one bulletin, read calmly, one item after another, as if they had all been the same event.

Solly Two Coats went into the diamond house at the northern port in a black hat and a beard, with three of his crew behind him mumbling scripture, and walked out twenty minutes later with a stone the size of a pigeon's egg in his coat lining. Nobody thought to stop men so obviously bound for prayer.

His cousin Marv rang from overseas that night. Straight over, Marv said. No stops, no fences, no cleverness. Bring it to me.

Grigor the Nail heard about it the way Grigor heard about everything. He telephoned Solly to recommend a bookmaker's in the city, a discreet place, good odds, no questions — and then telephoned Ike and Benno, pawnbrokers by trade and thieves by inclination, and told them exactly which doorway Solly would be standing in and at what hour.

Elsewhere in the same city, the promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter, Pretty Sam, out to a travellers' camp to buy a caravan cheap. Sam haggled badly and insulted somebody's mother, and a bare-knuckle man named Finn broke his jaw with one punch and left him folded in the wet grass. Which was a catastrophe, because Halloway had promised the gang boss Coldstone a fighter who would lie down. So Halloway put Finn in instead, shook Coldstone's cold dry hand, and swore on his own eyes that Finn would go down in the fourth.

Solly landed, ignored Marv entirely, took the stone to the fence Hersch, and went off to the bookmaker's with a locked case under his arm to put money on the fight.

Ike, Benno and their cousin Tulley made a mess of it. They meant to lift the case; they came away with the case and, because Benno panicked with a cleaver, Solly's arm as well. Grigor arrived shouting and shooting and chased them down the alley, and everybody scattered.

In the ring, Finn looked at the man opposite him and put him unconscious in the first round. Coldstone lost a fortune in ninety seconds and broke two of Halloway's fingers on the way out.

Marv flew in the next morning, found Solly's rooms empty and Solly's blood on a doorstep, and hired a bounty hunter called Ledge, who wore a long coat and never once raised his voice.

Grigor got hold of Solly at last and sawed the rest of the arm off to work the handcuff free of the case, and opened it, and found receipts, a passport, and no diamond at all.

Ledge found the pawnbrokers instead. He shot their car into scrap metal on a bridge and took Ike and Benno and the stone, which they had got from Hersch by methods best not described.

Coldstone fed Solly to his pigs on a Tuesday and had Halloway and Digby brought out to watch, so that they would understand precisely what the second fight going wrong would cost them. They understood. They told Finn: fourth round, son, down you go. Finn said nothing. That night Coldstone's men set fire to his mother's caravan with her inside it.

On the ring road, Grigor ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno in the back, and in the roaring minute that followed Ledge died, Grigor died, and Benno died. Ike sat weeping among the glass. Tulley, who had been waiting in the hedge, ran off with the only living witness — a filthy little dog that had swallowed the diamond off a table three days earlier and shown no ill effects.

Finn came out in the fourth round and knocked his opponent stone cold on the canvas. At which point the travellers who had been standing quietly all through the crowd took out knives and hammers and butchered Coldstone's men where they sat.

Halloway and Digby found Coldstone crawling behind the seats and shot him, twice each, to be fair about it. By morning every traveller was gone, and the field where the camp had been was empty except for tyre tracks.

A week later a dog was handed in at a pet shop on the high street, coughed twice on the counter, and produced a diamond the size of a pigeon's egg. Halloway and Digby, who had come in to buy a canary, stood looking down at it for a long, silent time.

Emlyn set down his glass on the mantel without drinking from it. "Four years," he said. "She told me in the hotel. And for what it's worth, I never thought much of your letters either. Overwritten. All those semicolons."

Wilder stood in the middle of his own sitting room like a man in someone else's. He had rung an hour before, incoherent, and Emlyn had come at once, on foot, hatless, as though answering a summons about a burst pipe.

They had spoken that afternoon too, in a bar off the square, though not to each other. Odile had come in out of the rain with her hair flattened and said, "It's finished, the marriage. I told him everything last night. All of it, from the beginning." She stirred her drink. Then, because she could not help herself, because the last useful thing she owned was a piece of information: "He's been publishing Rutherford, did you know? Your Rutherford." And Wilder, who had detested Rutherford for eleven years and had reason to believe Emlyn detested him too, felt the floor of the world tip very slightly, and understood that a great deal had been going on above his head.

Two years before that they had divided the crockery. It had taken forty minutes and had been almost cheerful. The rooms smelled of dust and boiled kettle, and Odile said the word *chore*, and Wilder agreed too quickly, and they carried the plates out in two boxes and left the keys with the porter, and the lease was surrendered on a Tuesday.

There had been a dinner, before that, at the house Odile kept with her husband. Lamb, and a claret Emlyn was proud of, and the two men talking racquets — court sizes, a master at school who could take a ball off the back wall, somebody's shoulder, somebody's brother's shoulder — until Odile sat with her hands in her lap and had no part in the talk at all, and rang for the plates to be taken, and was not thanked.

Before that, a restaurant, the two of them alone, and Emlyn ordering a second bottle and then a third, and baiting Wilder about the modern novel: nobody could write a scene any more, nobody could get four people into a room and out of it again, all interior, all weather. Wilder defended his clients hotly. Emlyn nodded and refilled and asked what the American was doing and never once, across three hours, mentioned the thing he had learned in the hotel.

Odile had gone back to the rented rooms the following week. She hung her coat on the nail. She said nothing whatever about the trip — not the desk, not the letter, not the corridor — and the afternoon passed exactly as the others had, and she left at six to be home for dinner.

In the hotel she had confessed. It had taken very little; Emlyn had asked twice, quite gently, and she had put her hands over her face. He listened to the end. Then he said, "You know, I've always been fonder of him than of you." He said it without cruelty, which was worse, and went down to arrange about the car. It had begun at the desk that morning, with the clerk holding up an envelope and Emlyn saying, mildly, *who writes to you in that hand?*

Long before the hotel there had been the child. She told Wilder in the rented rooms, standing by the window: her husband's, certainly her husband's. They talked it over for an hour and decided the rooms would go on exactly as before, and they did.

The rooms had come first, though — a quiet district, three flights, linen bought in a shop where nobody knew them, plates, a jug, a lamp with a green shade. It amused them to give the thing a household. They said so often.

And before all that, a party in the house of his closest friend, the noise of the drinks going on below, and Wilder taking Odile up the stairs to a room with coats on the bed, and telling her, in the dark, how lovely she was.

Odile had gone back to the rented rooms the following week. She hung her coat on the nail. She said nothing whatever about the trip — not the desk, not the letter, not the corridor — and the afternoon passed exactly as the others had, and she left at six to be home for dinner.

In the hotel she had confessed. It had taken very little; Emlyn had asked twice, quite gently, and she had put her hands over her face. He listened to the end. Then he said, "You know, I've always been fonder of him than of you." He said it without cruelty, which was worse, and went down to arrange about the car. It had begun at the desk that morning, with the clerk holding up an envelope and Emlyn saying, mildly, *who writes to you in that hand?*

Long before the hotel there had been the child. She told Wilder in the rented rooms, standing by the window: her husband's, certainly her husband's. They talked it over for an hour and decided the rooms would go on exactly as before, and they did.

The rooms had come first, though — a quiet district, three flights, linen bought in a shop where nobody knew them, plates, a jug, a lamp with a green shade. It amused them to give the thing a household. They said so often.

And before all that, a party in the house of his closest friend, the noise of the drinks going on below, and Wilder taking Odile up the stairs to a room with coats on the bed, and telling her, in the dark, how lovely she was.

His father lifts him and throws him into the deep end of the pool, and he goes down through the green light to the tiles at the bottom, and it is quiet there, and he does not want to come up.

He marries the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school, and there is money in it, more money than a peculiar weak child from an industrial town has any business touching, and there is a house and a swimming pool and a car with fins.

They dig bodies out of the cellars with picks and with their hands, and one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves, retching until something in him gives out, and they carry him away.

A fellow prisoner, a small furious man, promises him that one day, when the world is arranged again, he will pay someone to have him killed, and it will be about the scout, and it will be no more personal than weather.

He is housed with other prisoners in a disused abattoir in a great city, in a locker cut for the hanging of meat, five stories down in the cold rock.

The airplane goes into the mountain and everybody dies but him. His wife drives toward the hospital with a bad exhaust and the fumes fill the car and she arrives dead.

Lost behind the lines with a scout, in wet boots, with no rifle, singing a little under his breath.

He is home. Someone has hung a banner.

In the zoo the actress holds his hand and he explains, badly, what a mirror is for, and the small hands applaud, and the sky is a bruise, and he says: I have seen this before, I will see it again, it is happening now.

The green light of the pool. The applause. The banner. The beam.
